claims.text: The powder feedstock is cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi intended for laser-based additive manufacturing.
The proposed control system continuously monitors real-time thermal and optical sensor data.
The proposed control system adaptively adjusts laser power, scan speed, and scan strategy during processing.
Laser power and scan speed affect energy input, density, defect formation, microstructure, and mechanical performance in laser powder bed fusion of high-entropy alloys.
Rapid melting and solidification in high-entropy-alloy powder-bed fusion can generate large temperature gradients, residual stress, and cracks.
Machine-learning-driven closed-loop parameter control will produce a more uniform and controlled thermal field in AlCrFeNiSi.
The more controlled thermal field will minimize localized overheating and undercooling.
Real-time machine-learning feedback will narrow thermal gradients during rapid melting and solidification.
Narrowing the thermal gradients will suppress compositional segregation in AlCrFeNiSi.
Narrowing the thermal gradients will reduce residual thermal stresses in AlCrFeNiSi.
Adaptive control of energy input will reduce pores and hot cracks.
Higher energy density can increase printed density but can also produce hot cracking that parameter adjustment alone may not mitigate.
Closed-loop processing will yield a more homogeneous AlCrFeNiSi microstructure with lower defect density and residual stress than static laser processing.
The lower defect density and residual stress will improve both tensile strength and ductility.
Static-parameter laser printing of AlCrFeNiSi has shown compositional segregation, residual stress, and defect formation.
The effectiveness of the closed-loop system depends on sensor quality, sensor response time, and machine-learning algorithm performance.
